screens.body: If HTML is the structure of the page, CSS is the stylist. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how everything looks: colors, sizes, spacing, layout. The big win: your content stays in the HTML while all the styling lives separately — so you can redesign a whole site without touching a single word of content.
screens.heading: CSS is the stylist
screens.keyPoint: HTML holds content; CSS controls how it looks.

screens.body: There are three ways to attach CSS. Inline styles sit right on an element's style attribute — quick but messy. An internal <style> block in the head styles one page. An external .css file, linked from every page, styles the whole site from one place. For real sites, external wins: change one file, update every page.

check.question: Best choice for a multi-page site?

screens.heading: Three ways to add CSS
screens.keyPoint: External stylesheets style the whole site from one file.

screens.body: Selectors pick which elements to style. An element selector like p styles every paragraph. A class selector like .btn (dot + name) styles anything with class="btn" — reusable anywhere. An id selector like #header (hash + name) styles the one element with that id. Classes are your everyday tool; ids are for one-of-a-kind elements.
screens.heading: Selectors: picking elements
screens.keyPoint: Element, .class, #id — pick exactly what to style.

screens.body: Every element on a page is a box, and the box model describes its four layers. Content is the stuff inside. Padding is space between the content and the border. The border is the outline. Margin is space outside the border, pushing other boxes away. When a layout looks 'off,' it's almost always padding vs margin confusion.
screens.heading: The box model
screens.keyPoint: Content, padding, border, margin — every element is a box.

screens.body: Elements display in two basic ways. Block elements (div, p, h1) take up the full width and stack on top of each other like bricks. Inline elements (span, a, strong) flow inside a line of text, like words in a sentence. Knowing which you're dealing with explains most layout surprises.

check.question: Which one is a block element?

screens.heading: Block vs inline
screens.keyPoint: Block stacks full-width; inline flows in text.

screens.body: Flexbox is the modern way to line things up. Put display: flex on a container, and its children become flexible items you can arrange in a row or column. justify-content lines them up along the main direction; align-items lines them up across it. Centering things — once famously painful — becomes two lines of CSS.

options: Lays its children out in a flexible row or column
check.question: display: flex on a container…

screens.heading: Flexbox lines things up
screens.keyPoint: Flexbox arranges children in rows or columns with ease.

screens.body: A few properties do most of the visual work. color sets text color, background-color fills behind it. font-size controls text size, and text-align lines text up left, center, or right. Combine these with selectors and the box model and you can style nearly anything.

screens.heading: Colors and text
screens.keyPoint: color, background-color, font-size, text-align do the heavy lifting.
